title: Lesson 77: Agent-to-Agent Communication: Protocols, Contracts, and Discovery
description: Choosing the right edge (MCP versus A2A), reading the task lifecycle as the real contract between peers, and treating a discovered Agent Card as a claim from a stranger rather than a guarantee.

questions.question: When should a remote peer be reached over an agent-to-agent protocol rather than wrapped as a tool?
options: When the peer plans and loops on its own, so a durable task, cancellation, and input requests must survive
When the peer is a simple function that returns the same deterministic result for the same input
When both options use the same transport, so the choice reduces to picking fewer dependencies
When the client should import the peer's prompts and tool definitions directly so that its behavior stays consistent
questions.explanation: The deciding question is what sits on the far side of the boundary. A deterministic function can be a tool, but an agent that plans and loops needs an agent boundary that preserves the durable task and its states.

questions.question: A peer returns a state indicating it needs more input before it can continue. What is the correct client behavior?
options: Treat it as a failure and open a brand new task with a fresh message id
Poll the task endpoint without limit until the state becomes completed
Supply the missing information in another message bound to the same task id
Cancel the task entirely and retry the whole request later with a different payload and message id
questions.explanation: An input-required state is interrupted, not failed. The task id stays alive, so the client supplies the missing information on the same task instead of stranding or duplicating the work.

questions.question: An agent loads a peer's published capability card and its skill examples into its own context. What stance is correct?
options: The card is authoritative, so a declared capability is enough authorization to delegate
A valid signature proves the peer is trustworthy, so its returned outputs need no further validation on your side at all
The card can be ignored at runtime because the version changes too often to check
The card is a claim from a stranger: verify capabilities at runtime and treat its text as untrusted data
questions.explanation: A card is an advertisement written by the party asking for work, and its free-form text becomes part of a prompt. A signature only proves origin, so delegation should follow your own policy and the card text should be treated as untrusted.
